english: Happy New Year (lit. receive many blessings)
usage: Happy New Year (please receive many blessings)
Polite default; say to elders, bosses, anyone you respect at New Year
반말, to close friends and younger people
합쇼체; very formal, to a CEO, in a speech, or a written card
Shortened; also used at 추석 and other holidays, not just New Year
examples: 새해 복 많이 받으세요!
Happy New Year!
The all-purpose New Year greeting to almost anyone older or respected
할머니, 새해 복 많이 받으세요. 건강하세요.
Grandma, Happy New Year. Stay healthy.
Add 건강하세요 ('stay healthy') to an elder — the most-wished thing for grandparents
올해도 잘 부탁드립니다. 새해 복 많이 받으세요.
I look forward to working with you this year too. Happy New Year.
A polite work/colleague version pairing the greeting with 잘 부탁드립니다
nuance: 새해 복 많이 받으세요 literally means 'in the new year, please RECEIVE much 복 (blessing/fortune)' — 복 is a Sino-Korean word (福) for luck and good fortune, and the verb is 받다 ('to receive'), so you are wishing that blessings come TO the person. This is the single most important holiday phrase in Korea and you say it at 설날 (Lunar New Year) to basically everyone: elders, bosses, neighbors, shop owners. The default register is the 세요 form (honorific), which is safe for anyone older or not close; with friends and kids you drop to 새해 복 많이 받아. The huge English-speaker pitfall is the verb: learners say 새해 복 많이 주세요 ('please GIVE me blessings') by mistake — 주다 ('give') flips it into asking for blessings for yourself, which sounds absurd; it must be 받으세요 ('receive'). A second trap is the 직역 'Happy New Year' instinct to translate the English word 'happy' (행복) — Korean does not say 행복한 새해; the fixed idiom is the 복 받으세요 formula. Note it's also fine to shorten to 복 많이 받으세요 at 추석 and other holidays. When greeting an elder you usually combine it with a 세배 (deep bow); the words alone are the everyday version.

주다 means 'give', so this asks the listener to give YOU fortune — backwards and comical. The blessing flows toward the listener, so use 받다: 새해 복 많이 받으세요.
Translating literally as 행복한 새해 (보내세요).

Using 받아 with your boss or an elder.
받아 is 반말 and too casual for someone you should respect. Keep the honorific 받으세요; only drop to 받아 with friends and younger people.

english: I'll do the New Year bow for you
usage: I'll bow to you (New Year bow)
Polite-humble; announce it to an elder before you bow
Please receive my New Year bow
Said by some as they begin; lit. 'receive the bow'
I'll do my New Year bow
반말, to family elders you're close with
I will now perform the New Year bow
Formal; in a more ceremonial family setting
examples: 할아버지, 세배 드릴게요.
Grandpa, let me do my New Year bow for you.
Said as you kneel down in front of an elder on 설날 morning
세배 드릴게요. 새해 복 많이 받으세요.
Let me bow to you. Happy New Year.
The bow comes first, then the New Year wish while still bowed or rising
애들아, 할머니께 세배 드려.
Kids, do your New Year bow to Grandma.
A parent prompting children; note 께 (honorific 'to') for Grandma
nuance: 세배 (歲拜) is the deep, kneeling New Year bow younger people give to elders on 설날, and 드리다 is the humble verb for 'to give (to a superior)' — so 세배 드릴게요 is literally 'I'll give you a New Year bow', the polite way to announce you're about to bow. The verb choice is everything here: you 드리다 (humbly give) a 세배 UP to an elder, and the elder 받다 (receives) it, often replying with a blessing (덕담) and 세뱃돈 (New Year money). The big English-speaker pitfall is using the plain verb 주다 instead of the humble 드리다 — 세배 줄게요 is wrong because 주다 isn't humble enough toward an elder; with anyone you bow to, it must be 드리다. A second trap is the particle: you bow 할머니께 (honorific 'to', not 할머니한테 which is casual). Don't confuse 세배 (the New Year bow) with 절 (a bow in general, including the bows at a funeral or to ancestors) — all 세배 are 절, but you only call it 세배 at New Year. Also note the bow itself has a correct form (men and women fold hands differently); if unsure, just watch and copy the family — the words 세배 드릴게요 plus a sincere bow are what matter.

Calling every bow 세배.

english: Did you have tteokguk? (Did you celebrate New Year?)
usage: Polite; warm small-talk at New Year, 드셨- is the honorific past of 먹다 ('ate')
Offering a bowl to a guest; 그릇 = 'bowl' counter
Guess you're a year older now
The joke that follows — eating tteokguk 'adds a year'
examples: 새해 복 많이 받으세요. 떡국 드셨어요?
Happy New Year. Did you have tteokguk?
A natural pairing — the greeting plus this friendly New Year question
떡국 드셨어요? 한 살 더 드셨네요.
Had your tteokguk? You've aged a year then.
The running joke: eating tteokguk on New Year traditionally means you turn a year older
저 오늘 떡국 두 그릇 먹었어요. 두 살 먹었나 봐요.
I had two bowls of tteokguk today — guess I aged two years.
A playful reply leaning into the 'tteokguk = +1 year' idea
nuance: 떡국 is the rice-cake soup Koreans eat on 설날 morning, and there's a deep cultural belief that eating a bowl of 떡국 makes you a year older — so 떡국 드셨어요? ('did you have tteokguk?') is really a warm idiomatic way of saying 'did you celebrate the New Year / are you a year older now?'. It's light small-talk, not a literal nutrition question. 드셨어요 is the honorific past of 먹다 (먹다 → 드시다 → 드셨어요), so use it for elders/strangers; with friends drop to 떡국 먹었어?. The follow-up joke is 한 살 더 먹었네요 ('you ate one more year of age') — note Korean uses the verb 먹다 ('eat') for gaining age (나이를 먹다). The English-speaker pitfall is taking it literally and answering only about food, missing the New-Year-greeting subtext; the natural move is to smile and play along. A second trap is honorific consistency: if you ask an elder 떡국 드셨어요? but then say 한 살 더 먹었네 in 반말, the register clashes — keep it 드셨네요 to an elder. Also don't confuse 떡국 (New Year soup) with 떡볶이 (spicy rice cakes) — totally different dishes.

먹다's honorific is 드시다. To an elder or stranger say 떡국 드셨어요?; 먹었어요 is fine only with peers, and 먹었어? only with friends.
Saying 나이를 받다 for getting older.

usage: Polite default; said before 설날/추석 to almost anyone
연휴 ('consecutive days off') focuses on the holiday break itself
Swap in the specific holiday name when you know which one
examples: 미리 명절 잘 보내세요!
Have a good holiday in advance!
미리 ('in advance') is added when you say it a day or two before the holiday
고향 잘 다녀오시고, 명절 잘 보내세요.
Travel safely to your hometown, and have a good holiday.
Pairs naturally with 고향 ('hometown') since people travel for the holidays
연휴 동안 푹 쉬세요. 명절 잘 보내세요.
Rest well during the break. Have a good holiday.
푹 쉬세요 ('rest well') is a kind add-on for the holiday break
nuance: 명절 is the word for a traditional Korean holiday — specifically the big two, 설날 (Lunar New Year) and 추석 (Chuseok/harvest festival) — and 잘 보내세요 means 'spend (it) well', from 보내다 ('to spend/pass time'). So 명절 잘 보내세요 is the standard 'have a good holiday' you say to coworkers, neighbors, and shopkeepers in the days BEFORE the holiday. The key contrast is 명절 vs 연휴: 명절 names the cultural holiday (with its rituals), while 연휴 just means the consecutive days off — say 연휴 잘 보내세요 when you mean 'enjoy the long weekend' generically (works for any holiday block). The English-speaker pitfall is the verb: learners reach for 가지세요 ('have/possess') as a 직역 of English 'have a good holiday', but Korean uses 보내다 ('spend/pass'); 명절 가지세요 is wrong. A second pitfall is timing — 잘 보내세요 (future, 'spend it well') is said BEFORE/at the start of the holiday; afterward you'd ask 명절 잘 보내셨어요? ('did you have a good holiday?', past). Adding 미리 ('in advance') is common because people scatter to their hometowns right before the holiday.

usage: 반말, asking a friend if their family does it
Add -러 가다 for 'going in order to'
제사 = the death-anniversary rite; 차례 is the holiday version
examples: 저희 집은 설날에 차례 지내요.
Our family holds charye on Seollal.
A simple statement of your family's holiday practice
내일 아침 일찍 차례 지내고 성묘 가요.
Tomorrow we do charye early then visit the graves.
차례 (home rite) often pairs with 성묘 ('visiting ancestors' graves')
요즘은 차례 간소하게 지내는 집도 많아요.
These days many families keep charye simple.
간소하게 ('simply') reflects the modern trend of scaling it down
nuance: 차례 (茶禮) is the ancestral memorial rite families perform on the morning of 설날 and 추석 — food is set on a table for the ancestors and the family bows. The crucial collocation is the verb: you 지내다 a rite, never 하다. 지내다 here means 'to observe/hold (a ceremony)', so it's 차례(를) 지내다, 제사(를) 지내다, 결혼식 is 올리다, etc. — using 차례 해요 marks you instantly as a learner. The English-speaker pitfall, beyond the verb, is assuming every family does it — increasingly families skip or simplify (간소화) charye, and many Christian families don't perform it at all (they may do a 추도 예배, a memorial worship, instead), so it's polite to ask rather than assume. Don't confuse 차례 with 차레/차이 — and note it's unrelated to 차 ('tea'/'car') despite the 차 syllable. Pair words you'll hear: 성묘 (visiting graves) and 벌초 (clearing weeds from the grave before Chuseok).

english: We make songpyeon (shape the rice cakes)
usage: Polite-neutral; 빚다 is the verb for shaping rice cakes by hand
같이 ('together') — it's a family group activity
Same verb 빚다 for dumplings, common at 설날
examples: 추석에 가족이 모여서 송편 빚어요.
At Chuseok the family gathers and makes songpyeon.
송편 (half-moon rice cakes) is the signature Chuseok food
송편 예쁘게 빚으면 예쁜 딸 낳는대요.
They say if you shape pretty songpyeon you'll have a pretty daughter.
A famous old saying that comes up every Chuseok
저는 송편 빚는 거 잘 못해서 모양이 엉망이에요.
I'm bad at shaping songpyeon, so mine look a mess.
엉망이에요 ('a mess') — a relatable thing to say while helping
nuance: 송편 are the small half-moon-shaped rice cakes stuffed with sesame, beans, or chestnut that Koreans make for 추석 (Chuseok). The verb is the lovely specific 빚다 — used for things you shape with your hands from dough or clay: you 빚다 송편, 빚다 만두 (dumplings), even 빚다 (brew) traditional liquor. You do NOT 만들다 ('make') them in the careful family-ritual sense; 송편 빚어요 captures the hand-shaping. 빚다 is a regular consonant-stem verb (빚다 → 빚어요, 빚으면, 빚는), but learners often mangle the stem-final ㅈ and produce wrong forms. The cultural point: making 송편 together the night before Chuseok is a bonding activity across generations, hence the famous line 송편 예쁘게 빚으면 예쁜 딸을 낳는다 ('shape pretty songpyeon and you'll bear a pretty daughter'). A second pitfall is mixing up 송편 (Chuseok) with 떡국 (Seollal/New Year) — each holiday has its signature food. Note 빚다 also means 'to brew' and 'to cause/incur' (빚을 빚다 puns aside, 빚 also means 'debt' — different word, same sound).

usage: Polite-neutral; 입다 is the verb for wearing clothes on the body
입고 가다 ('go while wearing') for showing up dressed in it
한 벌 = the counter for a set/suit of clothes
examples: 설날에 한복 입고 세배해요.
On Seollal we wear hanbok and do the New Year bow.
한복 + 세배 — the classic New Year morning image
애기 한복 입혀서 사진 찍었어요.
We dressed the baby in hanbok and took photos.
입히다 ('dress someone') — the causative, since you put it ON the baby
요즘은 명절에 한복 안 입는 사람도 많아요.

english: We go to visit the ancestors' graves

갔다 오다 ('went and came back') — reporting it's done
We're going to clear the grave weeds

요즘은 벌초 대행 서비스 부르는 집도 많아요.

From Seoul you go DOWN to the provinces: 내려가요. 올라가요 ('go up') is for heading toward Seoul. The up/down is Seoul-centric, not compass-based.

Use 내려가다 ('go down there') when you're in Seoul heading to the hometown. 내려오다 ('come down here') is from the hometown's viewpoint. Direction depends on where you are.
Translating 'hometown' as 집.
집 is your house/home; 고향 is the region you're from / your parents' place. For the holiday journey it's 고향 내려가요, not 집에 내려가요.
